problems.title: Cube law
problems.statement: Dynamic power P ∝ CV²f, with voltage roughly proportional to frequency.
hints: P ∝ f³; energy per op ∝ f².
problems.solution: 1.73× the power for 1.2× the speed: each operation costs 1.44× the energy. Boost clocks buy speed at a steep energy price.

problems.title: Memory-bound at lower clocks
problems.statement: A memory-bound kernel runs 10 ms at 1.8 GHz using 200 W, of which 80 W is static and memory. Lowering the core clock to 1.2 GHz keeps it at 10 ms (memory-bound).

parts.prompt: Dynamic core power at 1.8 GHz, in W?
Energy saved per run, in J?

hints: Time unchanged; dynamic power scales with f³.
problems.solution: (b) 35.6 W. (c) 0.84 J per run, 42% of the energy, for free. Memory-bound workloads should run at lower clocks.

problems.title: Data movement energy
problems.statement: Horowitz's 45 nm estimates: FP32 multiply 3.7 pJ, add 0.9 pJ, 32-bit SRAM read 5 pJ, 32-bit DRAM read 640 pJ.

parts.prompt: Energy for SAXPY per element (2 DRAM reads, 1 write ≈ 3 accesses, 1 FMA), in pJ?

problems.solution: (a) ≈ 139×. (b) ≈ 1925 pJ, 99.8% of it moving data. Energy efficiency is reuse, exactly like performance.

problems.title: Power-limited throughput
problems.statement: A GPU with a 300 W limit runs a tensor kernel. At 1.98 GHz it would draw 400 W.

parts.prompt: Clock that fits 300 W, if power ∝ f³ (in GHz)?
Fraction of the advertised peak achieved, in %?

problems.solution: (a) 1.80 GHz, (b) 91% of peak. Heavy tensor kernels are often power-limited, not compute-limited; the spec peak assumes a clock you can't hold.

problems.title: Benchmark hygiene
problems.statement: Comparing two kernels on a laptop GPU.

options: Lock clocks (if allowed) or record them
Warm up until the clock and temperature stabilise

problems.solution: Stable clocks, warm-up and interleaving. Single cold runs measure the boost transient.

problems.title: Energy-optimal clock
problems.statement: A compute-bound kernel: time ∝ 1/f, dynamic power ∝ f³, static power 50 W. At f = 1, dynamic power is 100 W and time 1 s.
problems.solution: (a) 150 J. (b) 120.4 J. (c) $f^3 = 50/200$, $f = 0.630$: below that, static power over the longer runtime dominates. The energy-optimal clock is well below the fastest.

problems.title: Thermal throttling
problems.statement: Lab 9's 20-second run: first 2 s at 7.1 TFLOP/s, last 2 s at 6.2 TFLOP/s, SM clock 1.95 → 1.71 GHz, temperature 62 → 83 °C.
problems.solution: (a) 12.7%, (b) 0.877: throughput tracks the clock almost exactly, as it should for a compute-bound kernel. A benchmark run only in the first 2 s would overstate sustained performance by 15%.

problems.title: Performance per watt
problems.statement: GPU A: 100 TFLOP/s at 400 W. GPU B: 60 TFLOP/s at 200 W.
problems.solution: A 250, B 300 GFLOP/s per W. For a power- or cooling-limited datacenter (or a battery), B does more work per joule even though A is faster.

problems.title: What DVFS reacts to

options: the kernel is memory-bound (some GPUs lower clocks under low core utilisation)

problems.solution: Power and thermal limits, and on many GPUs also low utilisation. The data type itself doesn't, though heavy tensor work hits power limits sooner.

problems.title: Embedded budget
problems.statement: A Jetson-class module in a 15 W mode runs inference at 30 fps using 12 W.
problems.solution: 400 mJ per frame, 2.5 frames per joule. On battery-powered systems this, not latency, is often the spec.
